# RBE 549, Lab 6 Report

Tom Kazakov

*Lab synopsis: Build a pipeline for stitching a panorama out of two images. Integrate panorama stitching into the camera app.*

*![][image1]*  
*Figure 1\. Stitched panorama as the result of Part 1*

# Application Flow

1. Load two overlapping Boston skyline images  
2. Run SIFT keypoint detection on both images  
3. Run FLANN descriptor matching  
4. Execute RANSAC homography, mapping image 2 onto image 1 coordinate space  
5. Match visualization: side-by-side with green inlier lines and red outlier lines  
6. Perspective warp of image 2   
7. Overlay compositing, image 2 on top in the overlap zone; crop the output  
8. Save panorama to panorama.jpg

# Implementation Milestones

1. Feature detection and matching  
2. Homography estimation and match visualization  
3. Warp, composite, crop  
4. Compare built-in cv2.Stitcher and hand-built pipeline  
5. Interrate into the camera app

# 

# Interesting Observations

1.  SIFT vs SURF decision: SIFT doesn't require a special build of CV2 and provides more distinctive descriptors. Algorithm speed is irrelevant for the task at hand.  
2. Stitching without blending produces a visible seam due to edge aliasing and the lack of homogenized color and luminosity.  
   ![][image2]![][image3]  
   *Figure 2: Stitching artifacts without blending applied*  
3. To be pedantic, the panorama presented in the assignment description is cropped on the right, and additional filters are applied to the left image to help mask the missing pixels in the bottom middle of the image.  
   ![][image4]  
   *![][image1]*  
   *Figure 3\. Panorama from the assignment (top) and produced in the lab (bottom)*

4. OpenCV stitches images by applying perspective adjustments to both and also blending the seams. The result looks quite great.  
   ![][image5]  
   *Figure 4\. Assignment images stitched using cv1.Stitcher()*  
5. The built-in stitcher made extending the camera app's functionality trivial.  
   ![][image6]  
   *Figure 5\. Four images were captured and stitched using the camera app.*

# Gen AI Usage

1. Claude Opus 4.6 for general conversational ideation, probing around assignment requirements, formulating approach & strategy. Doesn’t produce code. Does proofread my technical writing.   
2. For general code-writing, PyCharm with LLM-powered contextual suggestions, boilerplate writing, spellchecker, and linter.   
3. Claude Code in PyCharm for interactive code gen and refactoring; used Opus 4.6. All code produced by Gen AI for this assignment was reviewed and verified, and also refactored or recomposed to varying degrees. Commit history in the repo can serve as proof of organic authorship: [https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/](https://github.com/kzkv/RBE549/commits/main/)   
4. Multi-agent setup in Claude Code: non-specialist Claude to sequence implementation plan; Briefer serves as a conversation partner to discuss each increment step; Drafter produces initial code to be reviewed, refactored, and acceptance-tested; Critic observes the increment and provides feedback for the material. For consistency and to avoid re-setup costs, the instructions are stored in the repo-level CLAUDE.md file.
